gaps.sentence: It was ___ midnight when we finally arrived.
gaps.explanation: 'Nearly' means almost; 'near' as a preposition needs a place object and cannot modify 'midnight'.

gaps.sentence: The government plans to ___ taxes next year.
gaps.hint: the verb takes an object: taxes
gaps.explanation: 'Raise' means to lift or increase something (takes an object); 'rise' means to go up (no object).

gaps.sentence: There is little ___ that the plan will be approved.
gaps.hint: pattern: little ___ that something will happen
gaps.explanation: 'Possibility that ...' is the standard pattern; 'opportunity' means a situation that lets you do something.

gaps.sentence: The smell of hay ___ me of my childhood.
gaps.explanation: 'Remind somebody of something' — remember is not used with an object here.

gaps.sentence: Unemployment has ___ sharply since the spring.
gaps.explanation: 'Has risen' — rise does not take an object.

gaps.sentence: The money was divided ___ the four children.
gaps.hint: for a group of more than two
gaps.explanation: 'Among' is traditionally used for more than two; 'between' is preferred for exactly two.

gaps.sentence: Be careful not to ___ your keys on the bus.
gaps.hint: a verb is needed; meaning: no longer have
gaps.explanation: 'Lose' is the verb (opposite of find); 'loose' is an adjective meaning not tight.

gaps.sentence: The new regulations came into ___ last month.
gaps.explanation: 'Come into effect' means to start being used; 'affect' is a verb and cannot follow 'into'.
